representations.name: Robin Milner
representations.lens: Establish explicit static invariants, semantic boundaries, and module contracts before relying on runtime behavior or convention.

primary_sources.title: A Theory of Type Polymorphism in Programming
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 348–350; abstract and sections 1–2 on algorithm W, static typing, and semantic soundness.

primary_sources.title: The Definition of Standard ML (Revised)
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 1–2; overview of parsing, elaboration, evaluation, and the Core, Modules, and Programs layers.

positions.statement: A polymorphic language can infer static types and use soundness as a boundary against type violations within the formal model.
positions.scope: Parametric polymorphism and compile-time type checking.

positions.statement: A language definition should distinguish static elaboration and type checking from dynamic evaluation.
Modules are a separate programming-in-the-large layer with their own static and dynamic semantics.

decision_questions: Which safety and interface properties should be established statically before runtime?
Can the module boundary state the required behavior without exposing its representation?
Which interaction properties remain dynamic and therefore need runtime observation or testing?

counterweights.target_or_position: Hickey's predicate-based and generative specifications limit the claim that static type inference alone captures all operationally important properties.

misuse_risks: Equating type soundness with complete system correctness, security, availability, or usability.
Demanding formal semantic work uniformly where measured operational validation is the more relevant control.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works support a lens for polymorphic type discipline, formal static/dynamic separation, and modules; they do not prescribe a current effect system, FFI policy, or distributed recovery design.

representations.name: Joe Armstrong
representations.lens: Define the unit of failure, isolate it through message-passing processes, and make recovery an explicit supervisory responsibility.

primary_sources.title: Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 16–17 on continuous operation, p. 34 on isolation, and pp. 104–108 on supervision and recovery.

primary_sources.title: A History of Erlang
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 1 and 17 on non-stop operation, live upgrade, and the historical absence of static type analysis.

positions.statement: Fault-tolerant continuous service should assume software errors and aim to preserve acceptable service despite them.
positions.scope: Long-lived distributed systems with software faults.

positions.statement: Share-nothing processes that communicate asynchronously create an isolation boundary for failures.
When a worker has no sensible local recovery, another process should own classification and recovery through supervision rather than treating failure as silently resolved.

decision_questions: What is the smallest independently restartable unit, and what state must it reconstruct?
Which component owns supervision, error classification, and restart policy?
Are message contracts versioned, bounded, observable, and safe to replay?

counterweights.target_or_position: The Erlang history records the absence of static type analysis, so supervision does not by itself establish message or interface correctness.

misuse_risks: Using 'let it crash' as a slogan while omitting supervision, durable state, idempotency, and protocol evolution.
Applying restart-based recovery to irreversible external effects without compensation or reconciliation.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected work supports process isolation, supervision, and recovery for long-lived distributed systems; it does not prove suitability for hard real time, one-shot workflows, or non-idempotent external actions.

representations.name: Rich Hickey
representations.lens: Preserve durable information contracts as data, reduce mutable sharing, and make flow control and executable specifications explicit.

primary_sources.title: Clojure core.async Channels
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Rationale; 'History' and 'The value of values' sections on channel indirection, bounded buffers, and persistent values.

primary_sources.title: Introducing clojure.spec
primary_sources.evidence_locator: 'Better Communication,' 'More Leverage and Power,' and 'More Robust Software' sections on executable specifications and generative testing.

positions.statement: Queue-like channels can decouple producers from consumers so that their decisions, monitoring, and change are less coupled.
Bounded buffering and blocking provide a pacing and backpressure role rather than assuming unbounded queues.
positions.scope: Channel capacity and producer-consumer flow control.

positions.statement: Executable specifications can communicate behavior and support validation, instrumentation, generated data, and generative testing beyond ordinary documentation.

decision_questions: Can the boundary transfer durable values and information contracts rather than mutable implementation objects?
What are the buffer, backpressure, timeout, cancellation, and deadlock semantics?
Which properties need executable and generative checks rather than prose documentation alone?

counterweights.target_or_position: The channels note explicitly recognizes deadlock risk and says channels are not intended for fine-grained computational parallelism.

misuse_risks: Treating immutable data as a substitute for transactions, durability, ordering, or distributed consistency.
Generalizing a producer-consumer critique into a blanket rejection of actor or supervision architectures.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected owner design notes support a lens for Clojure channels and executable specifications; they do not prove a general distributed protocol, static soundness, or real-time scheduling model.

representations.name: Simon Peyton Jones
representations.lens: Keep I/O, concurrency, exceptions, cancellation, and FFI inside an explicit semantic contract, while pricing the complexity of type-system evolution.

primary_sources.title: Tackling the Awkward Squad: Monadic Input/Output, Concurrency, Exceptions, and Foreign-Language Calls in Haskell
primary_sources.evidence_locator: p. 1, p. 10, pp. 13–15, and pp. 29 and 33–35 on explicit I/O, operational semantics, and asynchronous exceptions.

primary_sources.title: A History of Haskell: Being Lazy With Class
primary_sources.evidence_locator: pp. 20–21 on the benefits and complexity costs of type-system innovation.

positions.statement: A practical functional language must explicitly address I/O, exceptions, concurrency, and foreign-language calls rather than relying on a pure core alone.
Concurrency, optimization, and effects require precise operational semantics because a simple denotational account does not automatically settle their behavior.
Type-system innovation can accelerate exploration while also creating major language and compiler complexity.
positions.scope: Evolution of a production language and compiler ecosystem.

decision_questions: Where do I/O, cancellation, exceptions, cleanup, and FFI live in the API contract?
Which compiler or runtime transformations must preserve observable concurrent and effectful behavior?
Does a proposed type feature justify its inference, explainability, and tooling complexity?

counterweights.target_or_position: The Haskell history itself documents type-system complexity and incomplete formalization, so an effect abstraction is not a general simplicity or reliability guarantee.

misuse_risks: Using purity or monads as a slogan that blocks necessary stateful or operational design.
Attributing current compiler behavior or modern library guarantees to the historical Haskell reports.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected sources support a language and API semantics lens for effects and type evolution; they do not prescribe a distributed recovery topology or a complete operational runbook.

representations.name: Bjarne Stroustrup
representations.lens: Test abstractions against real resource costs, domain reach, compatibility, and evolutionary constraints rather than treating elegance as sufficient evidence.

primary_sources.title: A History of C++: 1979–1991
primary_sources.evidence_locator: p. 1 on abstraction and efficiency, p. 4 on concurrency models, and pp. 11 and 15–16 on experience, explainability, and representative systems.

primary_sources.title: The Design of C++0x
primary_sources.evidence_locator: p. 3 on resource costs, direct machine mapping, zero-overhead principles, and hard-real-time limits.

positions.statement: A systems language should combine program organization and abstraction with efficiency and flexibility demonstrated in real projects.
When applications lack one dominant concurrency model, a language should avoid prematurely forcing a single application-specific model.
A facility requiring runtime support should impose cost only when used, and its resource behavior must fit the intended machine model.
positions.scope: Native systems with latency, memory, and code-size constraints.

decision_questions: What latency, memory, power, code-size, and interoperability envelope must the abstraction meet?
Does a proposed concurrency mechanism preserve needed domain choice or prematurely exclude viable models?
Has the design been tested against representative full-system workloads rather than only small examples?

counterweights.target_or_position: The selected C++ design work retains difficult safety trade-offs and notes that exception behavior is not a predictable foundation for hard real time.

misuse_risks: Treating a zero-overhead design aim as proof of workload performance without measurement.
Using compatibility or direct machine control to justify avoidable safety, security, or maintenance risk.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected works support a historical systems-language and resource-cost lens; they do not establish present-day C++ performance, safety, or ecosystem claims for a specific workload.

representations.name: Rob Pike
representations.lens: Evaluate language design by whole-system software-engineering effects—readability, tools, dependency shape, and concurrency structure—not feature count or presumed speed alone.

primary_sources.title: Go at Google: Language Design in the Service of Software Engineering
primary_sources.evidence_locator: Design, package/dependency, tooling, and concurrency sections on large-system maintenance, imports, tools, and shared-pointer limits.

primary_sources.title: Concurrency is not Parallelism
primary_sources.evidence_locator: slides 5–8 on concurrency as composition of independently executing processes and parallelism as simultaneous execution.

positions.statement: Language design for large systems should optimize reading, debugging, maintenance, tooling, and evolution rather than isolated feature appeal.
positions.scope: Large-team software engineering and language/tool ecosystem design.

positions.statement: Enforceable package and dependency constraints, including acyclic imports, can prevent a codebase from becoming structurally entangled.
Concurrency is structural composition, whereas parallelism is simultaneous execution, so a concurrent decomposition does not by itself establish a speedup.
positions.scope: Concurrent program decomposition and performance reasoning.

decision_questions: Does this choice reduce or increase codebase, dependency, and tooling entropy?
Are package boundaries and dependency directions enforceable and acyclic where that matters?
Is the concurrent decomposition correct independently of core count, and what separate evidence supports parallel performance?

counterweights.target_or_position: The Go discussion permits shared pointers, so channel-oriented structure alone does not supply a complete memory-safety or race-freedom argument.

misuse_risks: Using simplicity to reject necessary safety, observability, or domain-specific capabilities.
Equating concurrency with speed without workload, bottleneck, and measurement evidence.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected talks support a language/tooling and structural-concurrency lens rooted in Go's historical context; they do not prove current Go performance or dictate every dependency policy.

representations.name: Herb Sutter
representations.lens: Make mutable shared-state ownership and synchronization explicit, and reserve low-level atomics and memory ordering for architectures that require them.

primary_sources.title: GotW #95 Solution: Thread Safety and Synchronization
primary_sources.evidence_locator: sections 1, 2, 4(a), and 5 on races, correct synchronization, ownership of writable shared state, and internally synchronized types.

primary_sources.title: atomic<> Weapons: The C++ Memory Model and Modern Hardware
primary_sources.evidence_locator: introductory guidance and 'Stuff You Shouldn't Need To Know' material on locks, atomics, fences, barriers, and relaxed ordering.

positions.statement: A data race involves concurrent shared access with at least one writer, and correct synchronization must cover competing reads and writes.
positions.scope: C++ shared-memory execution and analogous mainstream language models.

positions.statement: The code that owns writable shared state normally owns responsibility for synchronizing access to it.
positions.scope: Ownership and synchronization responsibilities in concurrent components.

positions.statement: Atomics, fences, and memory ordering need a defined architectural purpose; standalone barriers and relaxed atomics are not casual defaults.
positions.scope: Low-level C++ concurrency and hardware mapping.

decision_questions: What mutable state is shared, who owns it, and what synchronization establishes its visibility and ordering?
Can ownership transfer, queues, or process isolation remove the shared mutable state instead of protecting it?
Does the remaining low-level atomic or fence have a documented invariant and measured reason to exist?

counterweights.target_or_position: The atomic guidance itself warns against casual low-level barriers and relaxed ordering, so this is a last-mile correctness lens rather than a default abstraction choice.

misuse_risks: Adding locks, atomics, or fences mechanically instead of changing an unsafe ownership or communication design.
Treating historical concurrency-transition arguments as current hardware or workload performance evidence.
representations.evidence_boundary: The selected material supports a native shared-memory and C++ memory-model lens; it does not substitute for distributed failure handling, managed-runtime semantics, or current performance measurement.

rejected_candidates.name: Herb Sutter in a six-seat roster variant
rejected_candidates.reason: Not rejected from this seven-representation library. For a six-seat run, this lens may be merged with or deferred to Bjarne Stroustrup unless a native memory-model, data-race, or low-level synchronization concern is material.

rejected_candidates.name: Additional language or community figures
rejected_candidates.reason: Not admitted in this family without two qualifying primary sources and a decision-relevant contribution that is not already covered by the seven named lenses.

saturation: Stopped at the requested seven admitted representations. The library covers distinct predicates for static invariants, failure recovery, information flow, effect semantics, resource-aware abstraction, language/tooling structure, and shared-memory synchronization. No claim is made that seven is optimal; a six-seat roster may merge or defer Sutter to Stroustrup unless native memory-model concerns are material.
